content: 1. Planning for the implementation of standards in tuberculosis (TB) care for adolescents and young adults should ideally be overseen by expert committees specializing in TB care and adolescent health. This process should also involve adolescents and young adults who have been treated for TB, their families, and youth advocates. 2. The first step in developing effective TB programs for adolescents is to assess current gaps and barriers in delivering high-quality adolescent health care within TB programs. 3. Age-disaggregated TB data, indicators, and existing adolescent-friendly care models for conditions like HIV, sexual and reproductive health, and other health issues can provide valuable insights for planning. 4. Subsequent steps in the planning cycle include monitoring the implementation of adolescent-oriented plans and integrating these efforts into national reporting processes. 5. National plans to improve adolescent TB services should include the following components: Ensure that adolescents are managed by healthcare providers who are knowledgeable and skilled in addressing the unique needs of this age group. Conduct regular training for TB clinicians, nurses, and multidisciplinary staff on adolescent health to better understand and respond to their needs, values, and preferences. This includes providing confidential, nonjudgmental, and destigmatizing care. Train general and specialist healthcare providers to increase their awareness of adolescent-specific TB risks and the appropriate use of TB screening, diagnostics, and referral systems. Improve adolescents' access to TB services by offering after-school and weekend clinic hours, minimizing clinic waiting times, providing community-based or decentralized TB care, and facilitating easy transfers between TB care sites when adolescents relocate for school, work, or other reasons. Actively identify the broader healthcare needs of adolescents with TB by integrating TB care with other health services, such as comprehensive adolescent health clinics. In the absence of co-located services, establish clear referral pathways for common health concerns like reproductive health care, prenatal care, HIV care, substance use disorder treatment, immunization, and mental health care. Provide education and youth-friendly information accessible to adolescents, their caregivers, and the general public to reduce TB-related stigma and increase awareness about adolescents' susceptibility to TB, TB symptoms, and how to access TB testing. Address the psychosocial and mental health needs of adolescents with TB, including risks for depression and substance use. Routine screening for mental health disorders, counseling, psychological support, peer counseling, and peer support groups should be considered. Empower caregivers to effectively support adolescent TB treatment through education, counseling, and addressing family or caregiver needs, such as financial hardships. Collaborate with the education sector to develop policies that promote school engagement and retention for students with TB, facilitate TB screening and contact tracing, and provide adherence support for TB treatment when needed. Engage with local schools to build understanding of TB and support schools in responding positively to students with TB. Work with other sectors to address the basic needs of adolescents with TB and their families, including mitigating the financial impacts of TB and ensuring food security and continued education. 6. TB is a common cause or comorbidity in children with clinically diagnosed pneumonia. Studies indicate that Mycobacterium tuberculosis is identified in approximately 5–10% of children under five years old with pneumonia in TB-endemic countries. Limited data suggest that TB is also associated with mortality in these children. 7. Clinical features of TB in young children presenting with pneumonia, such as persistent symptoms, have low specificity for diagnosis. TB often presents with acute and severe pneumonia symptoms that are indistinguishable from other causes of pneumonia. Young age and a history of close or household TB contact are significant risk factors for TB in children with pneumonia, though only a minority of children with bacteriologically confirmed TB report close contact. 8. Poor nutritional status increases the risk of pneumonia from all causes and is both a feature of and a risk factor for TB. Malnutrition may also lead to false-negative tuberculin skin tests due to its impact on cell-mediated immunity. 9. Children with pneumonia who have prolonged symptoms, a history of TB contact, treatment failure, or recurrent pneumonia should be evaluated for TB disease. Bacteriological confirmation should be sought whenever feasible. 10. Children with severe pneumonia who are diagnosed with TB should be treated with a six-month regimen, as they present with severe disease. There is no evidence to support shortened treatment regimens in this subgroup. 11. Undernutrition increases the risk of TB by reducing cell-mediated immunity, while TB disease exacerbates weight loss and wasting, creating a vicious cycle. Approximately 19% of global TB cases are attributable to undernutrition. 12. Routine TB risk assessment, particularly a history of TB exposure, among acutely malnourished children, combined with improved referral linkages to TB services, could enhance TB case-finding and outcomes. 13. Integration and coordination between TB and nutrition services are essential to ensure that children and adolescents with malnutrition are routinely evaluated for TB. 14. Children and adolescents with TB disease frequently present with failure to thrive or weight loss. Severe malnutrition is a key risk factor for TB in children. Those receiving therapeutic nutritional treatment but not gaining weight should be evaluated for chronic diseases like TB. 15. Nutritional care is an integral part of TB care and prevention. All individuals with TB should receive TB diagnosis, treatment, and care according to WHO guidelines. Nutrition assessment and assistance should not divert resources from optimal TB care. 16. An adequate diet containing essential macroand micronutrients is necessary for the health and well-being of individuals with TB. Nutrition screening, assessment, and management are integral components of TB treatment and care due to the bidirectional causal link between undernutrition and TB. 17. Poverty and food insecurity are both causes and consequences of TB. Providers involved in TB care play a critical role in addressing these socioeconomic issues. 18. TB is often accompanied by comorbidities such as HIV, diabetes, smoking, and substance use, which have their own nutritional implications. These should be fully considered during nutrition screening, assessment, and counseling.
